items.prompt: Sam solves 30 problems in 3 hours. The linear model says 9 hours should give how many?
choices: 60 problems
30 problems
90 problems
items.explanation: Linear means output = hours times a constant rate, so three times the hours predicts three times the problems.

items.prompt: Which sentence states the linear assumption?
choices: Doubling the hours halves the errors
Doubling the hours doubles the output
Doubling the hours doubles the deadline
items.explanation: The linear model treats every hour as producing the same amount.

items.prompt: On a graph of output against hours, the linear model draws what?
choices: A line that rises then falls
A straight rising line
A line that stays flat
items.explanation: A constant rate per hour is a straight line through the origin.

items.prompt: Under the linear model, is there ever a reason to stop adding hours?
choices: No, more is always better
Yes, after exactly 50 hours
Yes, once output reaches double
items.explanation: The straight line never turns, which is exactly what makes the model dangerous at the far end.

items.prompt: A plan goes from 40 to 65 hours a week and expects 62% more done. What is that expectation based on?
choices: Output growing faster than hours
Output staying fixed whatever the hours
Output growing in step with hours
items.explanation: The expectation copies the percentage increase in hours straight onto output.

items.prompt: Why do people reach for the linear model under pressure?
choices: It has been proven for all work
It deliberately ignores tiredness and errors
It is simple and fits the first hours
items.explanation: Early hours do track the straight line, so the model feels right until the far end.

items.prompt: Does real output follow a straight line forever as hours rise?
choices: Yes, it only slows near midnight
No, the line bends past a point
Yes, if the person is motivated
items.explanation: Real curves flatten and can turn downward.

items.prompt: The linear model works best for which change?
choices: A small change around the usual pace
A huge increase held for several months
A change that doubles all hours
items.explanation: Near the normal pace the curve is close to a straight line, so the approximation is fine there.

items.prompt: A manager says "20% more hours means about 20% more done." Which hidden assumption is she relying on?
choices: Each extra hour costs the same salary as earlier ones
Each extra hour is spent on the most urgent task first
Each extra hour is worked by a different person
Each extra hour yields as much as the earlier ones
items.explanation: The linear claim only works if the output per hour stays constant, which is the part that tends to fail.
items.reference:
Straight line vs. real curve
linear: 40h gives 40, 65h should give 65
real: the line bends past a point
the model fits early hours, not the far end
Why: a constant output per hour is only a local approximation, so stretching it far gives forecasts the real curve never delivers.
items.learnMore:
The straight-line assumption

Output equals hours times a constant rate is a reasonable guess for a modest change. It fails when applied to a large or long increase, because the rate per hour does not stay constant.

Common mistake

Treating a model that works near the normal pace as if it held at any pace.
items.reflection: Think of a time you extrapolated a trend in a straight line (savings, a fitness plan, a to-do list). Where did it stop holding?

The team simply lacked enough total hours
Output per hour fell as the hours grew
The deadline was set a little too early
items.explanation: A big gap between hours and output points to a falling rate per hour, which is the failure of the constant-rate assumption.

items.prompt: What does diminishing returns mean?
choices: Each extra hour adds less than the last
Each extra hour adds nothing at all
Each extra hour subtracts from the total
items.explanation: The total still rises, just more slowly.

items.prompt: What does negative returns mean?
choices: An extra hour adds slightly less than before
An extra hour adds the same amount
An extra hour lowers the total output
items.explanation: Past the peak, the mistakes cost more than the hour produces.

items.prompt: In the assumed model (k = 2) output is 58 at 60 hours and 62 at 70 hours. Which region is that step in?
choices: Negative returns
Diminishing returns
Accelerating returns
items.explanation: The total rose (58 to 62) but by far less than the 10 extra hours, so it is still rising, only slowly.

items.prompt: In the same model, output is 62 at 80 hours and 58 at 90 hours. Which region is that?
choices: Diminishing returns
Negative returns
Linear returns
items.explanation: The total fell, so extra hours subtracted.

items.prompt: What is the turning point between diminishing and negative returns?
choices: The peak of the output curve
The start of the work week
The point where output is zero
items.explanation: At the peak an extra hour adds nothing; beyond it, it subtracts.

items.prompt: In the linear region, one more hour adds about how much?
choices: Far less than the hour before it did
Less than zero, so it subtracts output
About the same as the previous hour
items.explanation: The linear region is where the straight-line model is roughly right.

items.prompt: At the very peak of the curve, how much does one more hour add?
choices: About double
About a full unit
About nothing
items.explanation: The curve is flat at the top, so a marginal hour adds about nothing.

items.prompt: Past the peak, which lever helps total output?
choices: More hours
Fewer hours
More overtime pay
items.explanation: Beyond the peak, reducing hours raises the total.

items.prompt: In the assumed model (k = 2) output is 40, 50, 58, 62, 62, 58 at 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 hours. Between which two hours does the total first fall?
choices: 80 to 90 hours
60 to 70 hours
50 to 60 hours
70 to 80 hours
items.explanation: The total is 62 at 70 and 62 at 80 (near the peak at 75), then 58 at 90. The first drop shows in the 80 to 90 step.
items.reference:
Three regions of the curve
linear: each hour adds about the same
diminishing: each hour adds less, total still rises
negative: each hour lowers the total
Why: the peak separates a worse deal from the wrong direction, and only past it is fewer hours the better lever.
items.learnMore:
Diminishing vs. negative returns

Diminishing returns means the total rises more slowly. Negative returns means the total itself falls. The decision changes at the peak, which is why the boundary matters more than whether the line is straight.

Common mistake

Calling every slowdown negative returns, which hides the region where extra hours still help a little.
items.reflection: Where in your own work or study could you tell whether you were left of the peak or right of it, and what would have told you?

items.prompt: A team at 60 hours goes to 70, and later considers 85 (k = 2, peak at 75). Why is the second decision different in kind?
choices: It adds more hours than the first push did
It pays more overtime than the first push did
It happens later in the project than the first
It crosses the peak, so output falls
items.explanation: The first stays inside diminishing returns (58 to 62). The second crosses the peak and produces less (about 60) than the plan it replaced.

items.prompt: A tired hour makes a mistake. When is the repair time paid?
choices: On a later day, when it is fixed
In the same hour the mistake happens
Never, since mistakes cancel out
items.explanation: The fix is done after the mistake is found, which is usually a different day.

items.prompt: Which thing does fatigue lower?
choices: Focus and judgment
The number of hours in a day
The difficulty of the task
items.explanation: Tiredness degrades attention and decisions, which raises the error rate.

items.prompt: Net output is closest to which description?
choices: All hours logged in the week
Everything that was started and left open this week
Finished work that is correct and usable
items.explanation: Net output removes the effect of mistakes and repairs.

items.prompt: Sam redoes ten wrong problems from yesterday. What kind of cost is that?
choices: A bonus earned for putting in extra effort
Rework from earlier mistakes
Time saved by practicing
items.explanation: Redoing wrong work uses hours that produce no new output.

items.prompt: Why can total output fall even while hours rise?
choices: Hours stop being counted at night
Repair work outgrows new work
The clock runs slower when tired
items.explanation: Once repair eats more than the new hours add, the total declines.

items.prompt: Monday's mistakes cost hours on Wednesday. Why is that easy to miss?
choices: The cost shows up on a different day
Mistakes are invisible to everybody at work
Wednesday is always a slow day
items.explanation: A delayed bill is hard to connect back to its cause.

items.prompt: Tuesday's output looks normal after a long Monday. Does that prove Monday was fine?
choices: Yes, because Tuesday looks completely normal
Yes, because hours cannot affect output
No, the repair bill may not have arrived
items.explanation: Tuesday only describes Tuesday's hours.

items.prompt: Which model misses the delayed cost?
choices: One that also tracks repairs landing on later days
One that counts finished and correct work only
One tracking only hours against direct output
items.explanation: Without a repair term the model cannot see the bill.

items.prompt: In the assumed crunch model week 3 has 44 gross units and 10 units of repair carried in. What is the net output?
choices: 44 units
34 units
54 units
10 units
items.explanation: Net = gross minus repair carried in, so 44 − 10 = 34.
items.reference:
When a tired hour is billed
Monday late hour: makes a mistake
Wednesday: hours spent finding and fixing it
Monday looked fine, Wednesday looks slow
Why: the cost lands on a later day than its cause, so a model that only watches hours and direct output cannot see it.
items.learnMore:
Delayed rework

A mistake costs hours when it is found, not when it is made. That timing gap is why overtime feels productive while it is happening and shows its price later.

Common mistake

Judging a long day by that same day's output alone.
items.reflection: Recall a rushed task that came back to cost you more time later. How many days passed before the bill arrived?

Throughput, not comfort

Common mistake

Reading it as "never work long hours" or as a niceness argument that a pure output manager can dismiss.

Nowhere, it stays at 50

k = 2 gives 75h, k = 5 gives 60h

Why the bend point moves

Costly mistakes pull the peak earlier, cheap ones push it later, and months of compounding rework differ from one short push. Historical data supports the shape, not a specific number of hours.

items.prompt: Which evidence would best show your own team's curve bends earlier than average?
choices: A study of a different industry's hours
Net output tracked at several weekly hour levels
Total hours logged over the year
Surveys of how tired everyone feels
items.explanation: Only your own net output at different hours shows where your peak sits.
items.reference:
What moves the peak
peak hours = 50 + 50 / k (assumed model)
k = 2 gives 75h, k = 5 gives 60h
error-prone work and long horizons bend earlier
Why: the shape is general but the bend point depends on the work and the time horizon, so no single hour count transfers.
items.learnMore:
Why the bend point moves

Costly mistakes pull the peak earlier, cheap ones push it later, and months of compounding rework differ from one short push. Historical data supports the shape, not a specific number of hours.

Common mistake

Importing one study's hour counts as a benchmark for a different kind of work.
items.reflection: In your current work, what makes a mistake cheap or expensive to fix? What would that say about where your own curve bends?

items.prompt: Net output means…
choices: Total hours logged
Work started this week
Finished, correct work needing no redo
items.explanation: It is what remains after mistakes are repaired.

items.prompt: Hours logged stay at 65 for four weeks. What does that tell you?
choices: How much of the work was actually finished
How much rework the team ended up doing
How much activity there was
items.explanation: Hours measure activity only.

items.prompt: In the assumed crunch, weekly net output was 60, 46, 34, 22. What is the trend?
choices: It rose each week
It fell each week
It stayed the same
items.explanation: Repair carried in grew while gross output shrank.

items.prompt: The crunch total was 162 against 160 for normal weeks. What did it gain?
choices: Almost nothing, only 2 units
A lot more, about 60 extra units
A loss of about 98 units
items.explanation: 162 − 160 = 2 extra units for 100 extra hours.

items.prompt: The linear forecast was 260 and the model gave 162. How big is the overshoot?
choices: 98 units
62 units
38 units

items.prompt: Which metric should a crunch be judged by?
choices: Hours logged
Tasks begun
Net output
items.explanation: Only net output reflects what was actually delivered.

items.prompt: Week 4 net output was 22 against a 40 baseline. What does that show?
choices: Well above a normal week by then
Below a normal week by then
Equal to a normal week
items.explanation: By week 4 the crunch week was producing less than an ordinary one.

items.prompt: Why does "everyone is working hard" mislead?
choices: It proves that the work itself is good
It describes activity, not results
It lowers the number of mistakes
items.explanation: Hard work and finished work are different things.

items.prompt: In the assumed model week 2 has 52 gross units and 6 units of repair carried in. What is the net output?
choices: 46 units
52 units
58 units
6 units
items.reference:
Hours logged vs. net output
hours: 65, 65, 65, 65 (flat)
net: 60, 46, 34, 22 (falling, assumed model)
total 162 vs. 160 baseline, 144 after week-5 repairs
Why: hours measure activity, while net output measures finished and correct work, and only the second tells you what the crunch bought.
items.learnMore:
Counting what the crunch bought

Net output subtracts repairs from gross output. A crunch can look steady by hours and still deliver almost nothing extra, and the repairs owed after it ends belong in the total.

Common mistake

Reporting hours logged or work started as if it were finished work.
items.reflection: What does your team or class usually count as progress, activity or finished results? What would change if you counted the other one?

items.prompt: After week 4, 18 units of repair are still owed in week 5. What is the crunch total counting that debt, against the 160 baseline?
choices: 162 units, 2 above baseline
180 units, 20 above baseline
98 units, 62 below baseline
144 units, 16 below baseline
items.explanation: The total is 162 − 18 = 144, which is 16 below 160.

items.prompt: A report praises a crunch because hours logged stayed high every week. Which failure mode is this?
choices: Judging one single all-nighter like a pattern
Cutting hours with no plan
Measuring activity instead of net output
Importing a study's hour counts
items.explanation: Hours logged is an activity measure that hides falling net output.

choices: Measuring activity instead of results
Importing one study's hour counts
Cutting hours with no plan for the deadline
Judging one short push like a chronic pattern
items.explanation: The unit says to address scope, sequencing, or staffing, because hours were only one lever.
